title: A good thing to give thanks (Psalm 92:2)
hook: "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD", the psalm of the Sabbath day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lecha Dodi, and the room turning to the door. Your line was shake off the dust, arise. Today, the psalm sung right after the bride arrives.

Here's a small puzzle. There's a psalm the Mishnah calls the Sabbath's song. It says the Levites sang it in the Temple on Shabbat. Jews say it on Friday night and again on Saturday morning. Its title says, in so many words, for the Sabbath day. And then, in the whole psalm, the Sabbath is never mentioned again. No rest, no seventh day, no candles. So what makes it the Sabbath's song?
screen: `THE SABBATH PSALM.` → `SUNG BY THE LEVITES.` → `NEVER MENTIONS THE SABBATH.`

segments.voice: Psalm 92, in the old Jewish translation, opens with its title: "A Psalm, a Song. For the sabbath day." Then the first line: "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD." And it goes on: to declare your lovingkindness in the morning, and your faithfulness in the night. The whole day, held in thanks. Then the psalm notices something hard. The wicked spring up like grass; they seem to be winning. But grass is gone in a season. And the righteous? "The righteous shall flourish like the palm-tree." Like a cedar in Lebanon: trees that grow slowly and stand a long time. So maybe that's the Sabbath in it. Six days you watch the grass, what's fast, loud, winning this week. On the seventh you look at the trees, what's slow and lasting. The Mishnah offers another answer: a song for the time to come, for a day that will be entirely Sabbath. A world at rest. And a midrash tells a third story. Adam, it says, met his son Cain after the murder of Abel, and learned that Cain had repented and been given another chance. Adam was amazed and said: so great is the power of returning. And he sang this psalm. Some readers hear a second meaning in the opening line. The Hebrew for give thanks, l'hodot, shares its root with the word for confessing, admitting. It is good to give thanks. It is good to own up. After Adam's story, one word can carry both.
screen: `FOR THE SABBATH DAY.` · `MORNING AND NIGHT, IN THANKS.` · `GRASS, AND THE PALM TREE.` · `L'HODOT: THANK, AND CONFESS.` · then, large: `GOOD TO GIVE THANKS.`

segments.voice: Look back at the week and find one thing that was slow and good, a tree, not grass: a friendship that held, a habit you kept, a meal someone made. Name it, and say thank you for it, out loud or inside, to God if you pray, or to the person, or simply to the day.
L'hodot. To give thanks: the first word of Psalm 92's opening line, the Sabbath psalm that never mentions the Sabbath.
Your line: good to give thanks. A week of Maariv, Hashkiveinu, the omer, praying alone, Kabbalat Shabbat, Lecha Dodi and Psalm 92. That's six hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Psalm 92, followed by Psalm 93, closes Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday night and is said again in the Shabbat morning service as the psalm of the day; many congregations sing it.

chat.says: Psalm 92 is called the Sabbath song, but it never mentions the Sabbath. So why?
options: The Mishnah calls it a song for the time to come, a day all Sabbath.
It once had a verse about the Sabbath, but that verse was lost over time.
Only its title fits the Sabbath, so it was put there by mistake.
chat.meaning: The Mishnah reads Psalm 92 as a song for the time to come, a day that will be entirely Sabbath.
